  identity         ssh key {home}/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (proxy)
                   THE SANDBOX CAN ACT AS THIS ACCOUNT. It can push to any
                   repository this key reaches and authenticate to any host that
                   trusts it, for as long as the run lasts. No private key
                   enters the sandbox and your other keys cannot be enumerated
                   or used.
                   signing key {home}/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub (proxy)
                   THE SANDBOX CAN SIGN COMMITS AND TAGS AS YOU — vouching as
                   a human, for code it wrote itself, on any repository. snug
                   generates commit.gpgsign = true, so commits inside are signed
                   by default. The agent protocol carries no purpose, so either
                   pinned key can be used for either job.
                   git Some One <some.one@example.com>
                   gh some-one @ github.com
                   THE SANDBOX HOLDS A FORGE TOKEN FOR THIS ACCOUNT in a file it
                   can read (~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, 0600, on tmpfs — a
                   private copy, because gh REWRITES it on first use). A normal
                   `gh auth login` token commonly carries repo, gist, read:org
                   and admin:public_key; with admin:public_key anything inside
                   can add an SSH key to the account, an effect that OUTLIVES
                   the sandbox. Use a fine-grained token if that matters.
                   glab some-one @ gitlab.example.com
                   THE SANDBOX HOLDS A GITLAB PERSONAL ACCESS TOKEN FOR THIS
                   ACCOUNT in two files it can read
                   (~/.config/glab-cli/config.yml and ~/.netrc, 0600, on tmpfs).
                   A hostile process inside can do everything the token's scopes
                   allow on that one instance, as that one account, from
                   anywhere, until the token expires or is revoked on the host.
                   With `api` scope that is the whole account: it can add an SSH
                   key or mint another token, effects that OUTLIVE the sandbox.
                   A PAT may have no expiry at all. Any client inside that reads
                   ~/.netrc (git, curl -n, Python requests, Go modules) sends it
                   to that host unasked, on any port and over plain http too:
                   netrc is keyed by host alone. Use a narrowly-scoped, expiring
                   token if that matters.
